raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure due to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause. Earlier definitions restricted onset to the last month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum and required echocardiographic LV dysfunction; contemporary definitions are broader but still emphasize exclusion of alternative diagnoses and LVEF usually <45% [1-4]. PPCM remains clinically important because symptoms such as dyspnea, edema and fatigue overlap with normal pregnancy, delaying recognition, while outcomes range from complete recovery to cardiogenic shock, thromboembolism, transplantation or death [5-7].

Reported incidence varies widely by geography, ancestry and ascertainment. Older US population-based studies estimated approximately 1 case per 3000–4000 live births, whereas later administrative data suggested increasing incidence and substantial racial disparities [8-10]. The ESC worldwide registry showed PPCM across multiple ethnic and socioeconomic settings, with broadly similar clinical presentation but important differences in access to therapies and follow-up [11]. Established risk factors include African ancestry, advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. A meta-analysis found pre-eclampsia in 22% of women with PPCM and hypertensive disorders in 37%, supporting shared vascular mechanisms rather than simple coincidence [12].

Pathogenesis is multifactorial. Inflammation has long been implicated: in a prospective South African cohort, inflammatory biomarkers correlated with LV dimensions and adverse outcomes [13]. Experimental work shifted the field toward a vascular-hormonal model. Oxidative stress with impaired STAT3 signaling promotes cathepsin-D cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic, proapoptotic fragment; bromocriptine prevented disease in that model [14]. A complementary model showed that impaired cardiac angiogenic reserve and placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1) can produce PPCM, linking pre-eclampsia, multiple gestation and antiangiogenic stress [15]. Downstream, miR-146a appears to mediate endothelial-cardiomyocyte injury and may serve as a biomarker [16]. Genetics also matters: truncating variants, especially in TTN, overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy and are associated with more severe or persistent disease [17,18].

Diagnosis requires high suspicion in late pregnancy or postpartum heart failure. Initial testing includes ECG, natriuretic peptides, troponin when ischemia or myocarditis is considered, and urgent echocardiography to document LVEF, LV size, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation and thrombus. In IPAC, lower baseline LVEF, larger LV dimensions and Black race were associated with lower likelihood of recovery [19]. Biomarker studies suggest higher sFlt1 is associated with more severe symptoms and adverse events [20]. ECG is nonspecific, but abnormal findings are common and may provide prognostic information [21]. Cardiac magnetic resonance, coronary imaging or endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations, suspected myocarditis, ischemia or failure to improve.

Management combines pregnancy-safe acute heart failure care, postpartum guideline-directed medical therapy and cardio-obstetric planning. During pregnancy, loop diuretics, beta-blockers, hydralazine-nitrates and digoxin can be used when indicated; ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery. Severe presentations require intensive care, anticoagulation when LVEF is very low or thrombus is present, and early consideration of mechanical circulatory support [22]. After delivery, standard heart failure therapy should be titrated promptly, with lactation-compatible choices individualized. Bromocriptine, intended to suppress prolactin, improved outcomes in a small proof-of-concept trial and was further evaluated in a multicenter randomized study comparing short versus longer regimens; because it suppresses breastfeeding and may increase thrombosis risk, it should be paired with anticoagulation and used selectively according to local expertise [23,24].

Prognosis depends strongly on baseline LVEF, LV size, ancestry, comorbid hypertension, and speed of recovery. In Haiti, long-term mortality and incomplete recovery were substantial [25], whereas contemporary North American cohorts show frequent recovery but persistent risk in women presenting with LVEF <30% or marked LV dilation [19]. Subsequent pregnancy is a major counseling issue: relapse and maternal death are most frequent when LV function has not normalized, but recurrence can occur even after apparent recovery [26]. Current pregnancy-heart-disease guidelines recommend preconception counseling, avoidance of pregnancy when LV dysfunction persists, serial echocardiography and shared decision-making regarding contraception, breastfeeding and duration of heart failure therapy [27]. Overall, PPCM is best viewed as a genetically and vascularly susceptible heart exposed to peripartum hormonal, inflammatory and antiangiogenic stress; optimal care requires early diagnosis, multidisciplinary management and long-term surveillance [28-30].
